39.0.s.en: 1. The leader who loves the Law

39.0.0.en: 1 For he searches out the wisdom of all the ancients, and devotes himself to prophecies. 2 He keeps the discourses of renowned men, and enters into the subtleties of parables. 3 He searches out the hidden meanings of proverbs, and is conversant with the dark sayings of parables.

39.0.1.en: It befits the leader to realize his mission, so that he finds sweetness in his striving and in his continual progress in study and knowledge, especially of the Holy Scripture. This is what Bishop Ambrose presented to us when he said that the bishop must learn all the days of his life. There is only One who teaches and has no need to learn, and that is God.

39.0.2.en: And in contrast to that, he who gives himself to the study of the law of the Most High, seeking out the wisdom of all the ancients and occupying himself with their prophecies [1].

39.0.3.en: The leader counts himself an extension of the life of the ancients, so he does not stop learning from those who preceded him in the study of the Holy Scripture and in becoming acquainted with the prophecies of the prophets. Ben Sira reveals the law of the Most High and its distinction from human philosophies, bringing out that the law of the Most High, though presented as a personal dialogue between God and man, yet God, the Lover of mankind, wants His believers, whether leaders or people, to be an image of Him, bearing a heart wide, if possible, for all humanity. Therefore the believer is concerned to study the inheritance he has received from the ancients through the generations. But the philosopher is often occupied with his own selfish thought, as though he were the center of the universe.

39.0.4.en: v I desire to strive in learning so that I may be able to teach. For there is one Master (God) who alone does not learn what He teaches to all. But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God, their Teacher, what they teach others.

39.1.0.en: St. Ambrose He keeps the discourses of renowned men, and penetrates the marvels of parables [2].

39.1.1.en: By the renowned he means the people of God who fulfilled their mission in a spirit of godliness and witness to the life of faith.

39.1.2.en: v He mentioned with the greatest precision that the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were written on the breastplate of judgment. For bearing the names of the fathers written on the breastplate makes the priest ever think of the life of the early fathers. Then the priest walks blamelessly in the footsteps of the holy fathers who preceded him, contemplating their life, keeping away from vain imaginings, lest he take an unfitting step[1].

39.2.0.en: He searches out the hidden meanings of proverbs, and is occupied with the dark sayings of parables [3].

39.2.1.en: Ben Sira encourages his disciples, the seekers of wisdom, to travel in order to benefit from the wisdom and experience of others in the Lord. On another side he asks the believer to make his journeys through the ages, from Adam to the age in which he lives, where he studies God's dealings with the great fearers of the Lord, and examines the proverbs and the dark sayings of parables, as well as the Law and the Prophets and the books of wisdom.

39.3.s.en: 2. The role and characteristics of the leader

39.3.0.en: 4 He serves among the great, and appears before the ruler. 5 He travels through the lands of foreign nations, for he tests good and evil among men. 6 He sets his heart to rise early to the Lord who made him, and makes supplication before the Most High, 7 and opens his mouth in prayer, and makes supplication for his sins. 8 If the great Lord will, he shall be filled with the spirit of understanding. 9 He will pour forth the words of his wisdom, and in prayer give thanks unto the Lord. 10 He shall direct his counsel and knowledge, and in His secrets shall he meditate.

39.3.1.en: He serves among the great, and appears before the rulers.

39.3.2.en: He travels through the lands of foreign nations, and tests good and evil among men [4].

39.3.3.en: Whoever considers what is stated in this text [4-11] feels that the writer is presenting a portrayal of the life of St. Paul. Wisdom requires making journeys among cities [4], and among ages [3], and among the books of the Holy Scripture.

39.3.4.en: Kings and great men were drawn to the wise for the management of the affairs of the state or their private affairs or the upbringing of their children.

39.3.5.en: Their enjoyment of this fame does not lead them merely to hold fast to their personal experience, but they thirst to become acquainted with the experiences of others, even among foreign nations; therefore they are lovers of journeys.

39.4.0.en: He sets his heart to rise early before the Lord his Maker, and makes supplication before the Most High, and opens his mouth in prayer, and makes supplication for his sins [5].

39.4.1.en: This work, from the geographical, historical and scriptural side, requires of the one who desires wisdom to rise early, and stand in solitude with the Lord his Maker, and make supplication to Him and pray and ask forgiveness of his sins [5], so that he becomes qualified for understanding, knowledge and sound management.

39.4.2.en: The spiritual leader, more than any other person, needs the life of stillness and quiet contemplation, away from the atmosphere of service and teaching, for his own benefit and the benefit of those he serves, lest in the midst of the sweeping currents of service and the continual, relentless busyness he deviate a little. Then his service turns into routine or duty or into a merely formal service, or a service remote from the Spirit that has no spiritual effectiveness.

39.4.3.en: v Those who have been entrusted with works of goodness and the care of souls are obliged to bear to people a witness of the other life (the life of contemplation); therefore they must devote themselves to study and to contemplation of the truth and of eternal life.

39.4.4.en: And just as it is not fair that the life of contemplation should be a cause of hindering a capable person from carrying out the duties of the Church, so also it is not just that a person who is capable of the faithfulness of managing the affairs of the Church, because he is longing and burning for the life of contemplation and the inspiration of wisdom, should withdraw from the field of work and cast himself into the void of endless contemplation.

39.5.0.en: St. Augustine If the great Lord will, he is filled with the spirit of understanding, and pours forth the words of his wisdom (the Lord's), and in prayer gives thanks to the Lord [6].

39.5.1.en: As he receives wisdom as a divine gift he gives thanks to the Lord, for no gift is without increase except that which is without thanksgiving.

39.6.0.en: He directs his counsel and knowledge aright, and meditates on (the Lord's) secret things [7].

39.6.1.en: This study and this gift offered to him from above require walking uprightly, and delighting in contemplating the secret things of God, which are full of love and wonder.

39.6.2.en: v The eloquent define the orator as "a good man able to speak," for he must be without blemish in his conduct as in his lips (his oratory) so as to be worthy of praise, because the teacher whose words are not supported by his deeds loses all influence on his hearers.

39.7.s.en: 3. Teaching by the law of the Most High

39.7.0.en: 11 He shows forth the instruction of his teaching, and glories in the law of the covenant of the Lord. 12 Many shall commend his wisdom, and it shall never be blotted out. 13 His memorial shall not depart, and his name shall live from generation to generation. 14 The nations shall speak of his wisdom, and the congregation shall tell forth his praise. 15 If he remain, he shall leave a name greater than a thousand, and if he go to his rest, it benefits himself.

39.7.1.en: He proclaims the teaching when he teaches, and glories in the law of the covenant of the Lord [8].

39.7.2.en: John the Baptist was asked: "Who art thou?" And we would have thought he would say: "I am the one to whom Gabriel, who stands before the throne of God, came to announce to my father my birth," or "I am the angel who prepares the way before the awaited Messiah." But he said: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord..." This is my mission as a shepherd: to proclaim the voice of the Lord aloud, and to reveal the law of the Lord to my children, and to teach my brethren how to live! This is what distinguishes the shepherd, that he is able to teach others the way of the Lord.

39.7.3.en: Many commend his understanding, and it is never blotted out; his memorial shall not depart, and his name lives through all generations [9].

39.7.4.en: It befits the seeker of wisdom to realize that what God gives is not for him alone, but that many may enjoy with him the wisdom of God.

39.7.5.en: The nations proclaim his wisdom, and the congregation tells forth his praise [10].

39.7.6.en: If he lives long, he leaves a name greater than a thousand, and if he enters into his rest, his work is counted complete [11].

39.7.7.en: Successful ministry shows its fruit most after the repose of the leader, like the early patriarchs and the prophets and the saints in the Old and New Testaments and throughout history also. If his life is long, God permits him to be greatly honored in his life, and many benefit by his virtue. And if he enters into his rest, that is, rests in Paradise, the perfection of his striving and pastoral care is declared, and his memory also endures through the generations.

39.8.s.en: 4. The fragrant aroma of the Law

39.8.0.en: 16 I will yet declare my thoughts, for I am filled as the full moon. 17 Hearken unto me, ye holy children, and bud forth as a rose growing by the brook of the field, 18 and give ye a sweet savour as frankincense, 19 and flourish as a lily. Send forth a smell, and sing a song of praise. Bless the Lord in all his works, I have much to say, I will describe it in detail: for I am full as the full moon [12].

39.8.1.en: Ben Sira is in a state of illumination like the shining full moon, which no man can hide.

39.8.2.en: Hearken to me, you holy children, and grow like a rose planted by a stream of water [13].

39.8.3.en: It befits the one who learns wisdom not to limit his thought to the bounds of his people, but to seek that the nations proclaim the wisdom of God. For the seekers of wisdom are like roses planted by streams of water, who do not hold back the sweet aroma of Christ that is in them [13-14], and like incense that goes forth into the air, which all inhale. St. Clement of Alexandria spoke of God's care for man, how He created for him even the different kinds of flowers for his benefit.

39.8.4.en: v These flowers and herbs were created for our needs, not for us to abuse them in luxury. We leave room for a simple kind of indulgence, but it is enough that we enjoy their fragrance; we have no need to adorn ourselves with them. God the Father deals with man with great care, placing in our hands all the work of His hands for this one purpose, and as the Scripture says: "The principal things for the whole use of man's life are water, and fire, and iron, and salt, flour of wheat, and honey, and the blood of the grape, and oil, and clothing. All these things are for good to the holy."

39.8.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v By reading the divine writings the soul acquires great wealth if it receives them with love.

39.8.6.en: They are set like a spring for the thirst of the world, and everyone who is thirsty drinks life from them daily.

39.8.7.en: The divine books are blessed streams; all you who are thirsty, come, go and drink the water of life.

39.8.8.en: The rivers are for the drinking of bodies and animals, and behold the readings of the divine writings are for the drinking of souls; O distinguished one, give the body water to drink, and give the soul the Book to read and delight in.

39.8.9.en: It is thirsty for the spring that is in the books; it puts its mouth and drinks life from them every day.

39.8.10.en: The soul is tormented by the company of the evil world, and it is filled with senses and unlovely desires...

39.8.11.en: But if it opens the Book and reads with great love, it is enlightened at once and sees the beauty that cannot be comprehended.

39.8.12.en: And the light enters from the reading into the mind like a ray from the disk into the hollow of the eye.

39.8.13.en: And the wind of the Book blows from between the lines, and lifts the smoke of error from the mind.

39.8.14.en: The more love is joined to reading, the soul becomes pure and full of light and is not troubled.

39.8.15.en: The evil one envies and knocks (at the door) at once like a ruler, so that the Book may be made void by the disturbing thoughts of the world.

39.8.16.en: If the soul's love is joined to reading, it will despise and reject all activities for its sake.

39.8.17.en: And if love of the world increases, reading is made void, and endless deeds enter and the world comes to an end.

39.8.18.en: O soul that wishes to live well with God, bind your love to the reading of the divine writings.

39.8.19.en: And silence the troubled banquets of the world, and make them void, and remove them from your mind.

39.8.20.en: And listen to the Book, which cauterizes the wound, and heals the sickness, and cares for the soul and bandages it and restores it by healing[2].

39.8.21.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh Send forth your fragrance like incense, and flourish like the lily.

39.8.22.en: And spread abroad your fragrance, and sing a song of praise, and bless the Lord for all His works [14].

39.8.23.en: The lifting up of incense during worship points to God's pleasure in the offering of prayer, and it is an ancient tradition whose beginning is not known, and extends so that we see it in heaven practised by the bodiless priests. David the prophet wrote: "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense" (Ps 141:2). And Malachi prophesied that the Gentiles would use it in worship: "For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering" (Mal 1:11). One of the gifts offered to the Child Jesus by the Magi was incense.

39.8.24.en: v It befits us to seek "incense" (see Sir 39:14), but not any kind of incense, but that pure kind. The high priest does not wish to take anything dark and base, but asks what is pure. He also asks for galbanum (a resinous gum), which by nature drives away harmful snakes by the strength of its smell. And he asks for "myrrh," for he wants our words and deeds to be holy and pure. He also asks for onyx or the Yemeni agate (onycha) (Ex 30:34), which covers some animals as a kind of shield to protect them so that no harm touches them[3].

39.9.s.en: 5. The Law of the Most High and praise

39.9.0.en: 20 And magnify his name, and give thanks unto him with praise, with the songs of your lips and with harps, and in praising him you shall say thus in confession. 21 All the works of the Lord are exceeding good, and all his commandments are accomplished in their time, and all of them are sought in their season. 22 At his word the water stood as an heap, and the receptacles of waters at the word of his mouth. 23 At his commandment is all his good pleasure, and none can hinder when he will save. 24 The works of all flesh are before him, and nothing can be hid from his eyes. 25 He seeth from everlasting to everlasting, and there is nothing wonderful before him. 26 A man cannot say: "What is this?" or "Wherefore is that?" for all things are created for their uses. 27 His blessing overflowed like a river, learning wisdom is not separated from the practice of praise [15-35]. It is not a subject of dry theoretical debate but a subject of fellowship with the heavenly ones in their praises. The man of God praises Him for His wonderful works in creation, and is not troubled by the calamities that come, but they drive him to cling to the fear of the Lord and his rejection of evil.

39.9.1.en: Magnify His name, and give thanks to Him with praise, with the songs of your lips and with harps, and say thus in thanksgiving: [15]

39.9.2.en: v The confession of sins is the ordinary confession known to you. There is no need for me to speak of the reasons for its use. Therefore it befits us to look at confession in the praise of God and the proofs of it.

39.9.3.en: People are accustomed to the call to "confession" of sins, and every time they hear the reader say the words: "Confess," they beat their breasts, with a murmur accompanied by an uproar within their consciences, as they remember what they must do.

39.9.4.en: This often happens, yet it is not always meant as confession of sins. Sometimes a person speaks of confession in praise, as in that passage in the Holy Scripture where it says: "Confess to the Lord, and say thus: The works of the Lord are all exceeding good"... It is clear that this is a confession of praise to the Lord and not of your offenses... Certainly the Lord Jesus did not commit sin, yet it is said in the Gospel: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth," and He completed the speech with praise: "because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes. Even so, Father: for so it seemed good in thy sight" (Mt 11:25-26). This is the confession of one who praises God, not of one who accuses himself[4].

39.9.5.en: St. Augustine All things are the works of the Lord and they are exceeding good, and all His commandments are accomplished in their times.

39.9.6.en: No one can say: "What is this? And why is that?"

39.9.7.en: For every question will be answered in its appointed time [16].

39.9.8.en: All the works of the Lord are exceeding good, but sin has corrupted man's sight so that he sees what is good as bad.

39.9.9.en: v It befits us to bless the Creator of all things before we partake of food, and so also at celebrations when we enjoy His gifts that He created. It is fitting to sing psalms directed to Him. In truth, to sing a psalm in harmony is a blessing; it is a work of self-control. The Apostle calls the psalm a spiritual praise (Col 3:6; Eph 5:9). Again, it is a holy duty to give thanks to God for His kindnesses and the love He shows us, before we sleep. The Scripture says: "Give thanks to Him with praise, with the songs of the lips, for His commandments that bring forth all kindness, and there is no lack in His salvation"[5].

39.9.10.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v God is good, without passions, and does not change. Man accepts this saying as a true fact that God does not change, but he is perplexed, asking how God rejoices in the righteous and leaves the wicked, and is angry with sinners and shows them mercy if they repent?! And the answer to this is that God neither rejoices nor is angry, for joy and anger are passions, and it is absurd to think that the Godhead can be benefited or harmed by human behavior. God is good, and does nothing but good. He harms no one and remains as He is always. But as for us, when we are good we enter into fellowship with God by becoming like Him. And when we become wicked we deprive ourselves of God by not being like Him.

39.9.11.en: When we live a virtuous life we belong to God, and when we become wicked we abandon Him. This does not mean that He is angry with us, but with our sins, which hide His face from us and bind us to the troublers, who are the demons.

39.9.12.en: But (at repentance), by prayers and doing good (with faith in Him) we obtain the removal of sins. This does not mean that we appease Him and change Him, but by these works of ours and our return to Him we are healed (by His grace) of the evil that is in ourselves, and become able to be partakers with God in His goodness. So also with the saying "God leaves the wicked": we are like one who says that the sun hides itself from those who have lost their sight[6].

39.9.13.en: St. Anthony the Great At His word the water stood as an heap.

39.9.14.en: And at the word of His mouth were the receptacles of waters [17].

39.9.15.en: Here he refers to the separation of the oceans from the earth in creation (Gen 1:9-10).

39.9.16.en: At His command everything is accomplished according to His good pleasure, and no one can diminish His salvation [18].

39.9.17.en: v By the tenderness of our Creator there are many ways of salvation, those which calm spirits and lead them toward heaven[7].

39.9.18.en: St. Anthony the Great v After the first man was deceived by the serpent, and received counsel in sin, and by sin met death, and by death misery, God did not forget him. The goodness of God did not forget us, in spite of our dryness toward the tenderness of God and our violent resistance to the Maker of good things. Yet we cannot blot out His love for us, for we have risen from death, and have become alive by our Lord Jesus Christ Himself... And it was not enough for Him to call us to life anew, but He prepares us for eternal rest, which in the greatness of its joy surpasses all human thought[8].

39.9.19.en: St. Basil the Great The works of all men are before Him, and nothing can be hid from His eyes [19].

39.9.20.en: His sight extends to them from age to age, and nothing is wonderful to Him [20].

39.9.21.en: God formed man, and knows all his thoughts and works, and man must realize this well, for the eye of God follows him to the farthest place, and at all times "from everlasting to everlasting," and nothing is too hard for Him.

39.9.22.en: No one can say: "What is this? And why is that?"

39.10.0.en: For all things were created to perform their work [21].

39.10.1.en: God created everything for a purpose, so that even what we see as harmful is in reality useful. St. Jerome has an essay on the importance of insects, whose existence some object to, yet which play a role among the rest of the creatures.

39.11.0.en: His blessing overflowed like a river, covered the dry land, and watered it like a flood [22].

39.11.1.en: Perhaps in this there was a reference to the River Nile, whose flood nourished the land in the Nile basin with much fertile silt, so that the land produced a double harvest.

39.12.s.en: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

39.12.0.en: 28 And watered the dry land like a flood. So shall the nations inherit his wrath, 29 as he hath turned the waters into dry land. His ways are straight unto the holy; so are they stumblingblocks unto the wicked. 30 For the good are good things created from the beginning, so evil things for sinners. 31 The principal things for the whole use of man's life are water, fire, iron, and salt, flour of wheat, honey, milk, and the blood of the grape, and oil, and clothing. 32 All these things are for good to the godly; so to the sinners they are turned into evil. 33 There be spirits that are created for vengeance, which in their fury lay on sore strokes. 34 In the time of destruction they pour out their force, and appease the wrath of him that made them. 35 Fire, and hail, and famine, and death, all these were created for vengeance. 36 The teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions, serpents, and the sword, punishing the wicked to destruction. 37 They shall rejoice in his commandment, and they shall be ready upon earth, when need is; and when their time is come they shall not transgress his word. 38 Therefore from the beginning I was resolved, and I thought on these things, and have left them in writing. 39 All the works of the Lord are good, and he will give every needful thing in due season. 40 So that a man cannot say, "This is worse than that": for in time they shall all be well approved. 41 And therefore praise ye the Lord with the whole heart and mouth, and bless the name of the Lord.

39.12.1.en: As He turns sweet waters into salt, so the heathen inherit His wrath [23].

39.12.2.en: God pours out His wrath upon the stubborn, and because of stubbornness the earth is defiled, so that sweet waters are turned into salt.

39.12.3.en: Just as His ways are straight for the holy, so they are a stumblingblock for the wicked [24].

39.12.4.en: The divine commandments, which are a cause of blessing for His saints, are a cause of condemnation for the wicked.

39.12.5.en: v The texts of the Holy Scripture lead us to understand that a stumblingblock is everything that draws us away from true godliness in any form of deviation, or committing faults, or failing to observe godliness.

39.12.6.en: In general it is everything that hinders us from keeping the commandment, even if the result of that is death[9].

39.12.7.en: St. Basil the Great Just as good things were created from the beginning for the good, so evil things for sinners [25].

39.12.8.en: The divine works that the saints see as good and so praise Him are the very ones that sinners see as evil. Nothing is unclean, but "unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled" (Titus 1:15). So where a man is pure, that is, pure in heart, he sees everything in God's creation as pure. And St. Jerome[10] defines the pure heart as the one at which God looks. For by the holy God the heart is sanctified, and God's pure look at everyone and everything becomes its own.

39.12.9.en: As for how it is purified, St. Augustine says: [The truth is that all are unclean, those who have not been purified by faith in Christ, as the passage says: "purifying their hearts by faith" (Acts 15:9)[11].]

39.12.10.en: The basic needs of man's life are: water, fire, iron, salt, flour of wheat, milk, honey, the blood of the grape, olive oil and clothing [26].

39.12.11.en: He speaks of the principal elements in man's life as the Lord provided them for man; these elements may be used for evil, for the water that quenches thirst can destroy, as happens in floods. And iron is used to make instruments of battle. And salt, for preserving, if increased in the food spoils it. Wheat and milk and honey, which points to prosperity, are misused by the covetous. And the blood of the grape, that is, wine, points to gladness and joy, and the wicked get drunk with it.

39.12.12.en: All these things are good for the godly, but they turn to evil for sinners [27].

39.12.13.en: Foods differ from one country to another, and from one generation to another; the principal needs such as water, fire, salt, etc., do not change.

39.12.14.en: v For healing, medicine may make use of some flowers in order to extract from them some ointments and perfumes, and this cannot be overlooked. And if some ask: What use are these flowers to those who do not use them? Let them know that ointments are made from certain kinds of flowers and they are very useful...

39.12.15.en: All these exist so that we may benefit from them and use them[12].

39.12.16.en: St. Clement of Alexandria There are spirits that were created for vengeance, and in His (the Lord's) wrath they increase their scourges, and in the time of destruction they pour out their force, and appease the wrath of their Maker [28].

39.12.17.en: Perhaps it refers to destructive storms, while there are beneficial winds, and gentle winds may turn into destructive storms as a discipline for the wicked.

39.13.0.en: Fire, hail, famine and death, all these were created for vengeance [29].

39.13.1.en: Among the fruits of sin are suffering hunger and thirst and calamities, because it isolates man from God, the source of his true satisfaction and quenching.

39.13.2.en: v Let us return again to the same prophet (Amos) whom we heard at the beginning of the discourse: "And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city: one piece was rained upon, and the piece whereupon it rained not withered. So two or three cities wandered unto one city, to drink water; but they were not satisfied: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the Lord" (Amos 4:7-8).

39.13.3.en: We must learn, then, that because of our distance from the Lord, and our unconcern for His ways, God has caused us those wounds.

39.13.4.en: He does not seek our destruction, but rather strives to bring us back to the right way, just as good parents care for their children with firmness, rebuking them when they do something wrong, not because they seek to harm them, but rather because they wish to lead them from childish neglect and the sins of youth to the attainment of mature alertness[13].

39.14.0.en: St. Basil the Great The teeth of wild beasts, scorpions, serpents and the avenging sword for the destruction of the wicked [30].

39.14.1.en: Man was master of the earthly creatures, and the wild beasts were subject to Adam and Eve; but when man disobeyed God in stubbornness, these animals became terrifying to him, and man even came to kill his brethren with the sword. When the people murmured in the wilderness He let the fiery serpents bite them (Num 21:5-6), and when some children mocked Elisha the prophet He allowed two bears to kill forty-two of them, and when the king of Assyria sent pagan people to dwell in the land of Canaan after his taking the people of Israel captive, God sent lions among them to devour them (2 Kgs 17:24, 26). What are these beasts that are let loose upon us but the sins from which God keeps us as long as we are in His presence responding to His voice; for if we give Him the back and not the face He lets the beasts bereave us of our children, that is, our inner fruits, and gnaw our cattle, that is, corrupt our body?!

39.14.2.en: Origen says: [Many are the swords that pass through our land if we do not keep the law of the Lord and follow His commandments! Let each one enter into himself, and contemplate within himself, lest our land, that is our body, be stirred up by a spirit of fornication or disturbed by a spirit of anger and agitation, or by a movement of covetousness, or by the bow of lust and pleasures... This the Apostle Paul knows, for he says: "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God" (2 Cor 10:5), so that we do not submit to this sword and those wars, but the Lord keeps our land in safety.]

39.15.0.en: They rejoice in carrying out His commandment, and make ready for His service upon earth, and when the time comes they do not transgress His word [31].

39.15.1.en: By natural instinct the wild beasts are subject to the will of God, and do not transgress His word, for God sometimes uses them for discipline.

39.15.2.en: St. Basil the Great[14] sees that it befits the believer not to fear wild and poisonous animals, etc., for God has permitted them for our discipline as well as for our benefit. The animals bear witness to faith. Have you confidence in God? "Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder (a malignant kind of serpent): the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet" (Ps 91:13). By faith you have power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. Do you not see that the viper that fastened on the hand of the Apostle Paul as he gathered sticks did not harm him (Acts 28:3), because it found the saint full of faith? If you have faith, do not fear the animals more than you fear your unbelief, which makes you liable to destruction.

39.16.0.en: Therefore from the beginning I was resolved and determined, and I left this in writing: [32]

39.17.0.en: All the works of the Lord are good, and He will supply every need in its hour [33].

39.17.1.en: v Be a herald of the goodness of God, for God rules over you in spite of your unworthiness. Although your debt to Him is very great, He is not seen demanding of you full payment; and through your very small works He gives you great rewards. Do not call God just, for His justice is not declared in the things that concern you. And if David calls Him just and upright (Ps 25:8; 145:17), His Son declares to us that He is good and compassionate[15].

39.17.2.en: St. Isaac the Syrian v His light cannot be hidden, nor can His glory remain without a witness, nor can His goodness go unenjoyed, nor can all that pertains to the divine nature remain unused for the benefit of man, that he may enjoy it and share in it. For if man came into being for this purpose, that is, to share with God in His goodness, then certainly in his creation he was given the capacity to enjoy all that is good. So the eye enjoys seeing the true light by virtue of the ray implanted in it naturally, which draws to itself what is like it by its innate power. Likewise there had to be a likeness of human nature to the divine so that through this likeness it might be joined with what is akin to it. Irrational creatures, whether those that live in water or in air, had to have an order adapted to the environment surrounding each creature, so that each might find its kind and what is akin to it, one in the air and another in the water. So too man, who came into being to enjoy the goodness of God, had to have something in his nature resembling that in which he would share. For this reason man was endowed with life and reason and wisdom and all the attributes that befit God, so that through all of these there might arise in him the desire for what is akin to him[16].

39.18.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa No one can say: "This is worse than that," for all things are well pleasing in their time [34].

39.18.1.en: God's providence is surpassing; all things work out for good as long as we use them fittingly and at the proper time.

39.19.0.en: So now sing with all your heart and voice, and bless the name of the Lord [35].

39.19.1.en: Ben Sira speaks here of God's plan of salvation as the supreme work of God, which He accomplished by the incarnation of the Word of God and by offering Himself as a sacrifice for humanity.

39.20.s.en: Your Law makes my heart rejoice!

39.20.0.en: v Grant me to be faithful in devoting my life to Your Law.

39.20.1.en: That I may draw from the experiences of the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, enjoy the experiences of the saints and understand their wisdom.

39.20.2.en: I rise early to You with every morning, I confess my sins and ask for Your wisdom.

39.20.3.en: I seek Your work even among strangers, O Lover of all nations!

39.20.4.en: v I glory in Your covenant, and desire the salvation of all humanity. I am careful of every moment to enjoy Your wisdom, so my soul will find rest when it departs from the body! Your wisdom turns my life into a full moon in its light!

39.20.5.en: Your wisdom is a spring of living water that waters the roses planted within me.

39.20.6.en: v Your Law turns my life into a spiritual harp.

39.20.7.en: Your Holy Spirit plays upon it the song of wisdom and the melody of love!

39.20.8.en: You reveal to me the mystery of Your care for humanity.

39.20.9.en: All things work for the edification of Your beloved children, and for the one who resists the truth, things are turned to his discipline.

39.20.10.en: Those who oppose You suffer from it as a harsh discipline.

39.20.11.en: While Your children count it as surpassing gifts, You are wonderful in Your care and Your plan and Your divine ordering!
